                                                        Abstract
     In the classic point location problem, one is given an arbitrary dataset X ⊂ Rd of n points with
     query access to an unknown halfspace f : Rd → {0, 1}, and the goal is to learn the label of every
     point in X. This problem is extremely well-studied and a nearly-optimal O(d     e log n) query algo-
     rithm is known due to Hopkins-Kane-Lovett-Mahajan (FOCS 2020). However, their algorithm is
     granted the power to query arbitrary points outside of X (point synthesis), and in fact without this
     power there is an Ω(n) query lower bound due to Dasgupta (NeurIPS 2004). Nonetheless, query
     access to arbitrary synthesized data points is unrealistic in many contexts.
          Our objective in this work is to design efficient algorithms for learning halfspaces without
     point synthesis. To circumvent the Ω(n) lower bound, we consider learning halfspaces whose
     normal vectors come from a known set of size D, and show tight bounds of Θ(D + log n). As a
     corollary, we obtain an optimal O(d + log n) query deterministic learner for the fundamental class
     of decision stumps (depth-one decision trees, or axis-aligned halfspaces), closing a previous gap of
     O(d log n) vs. Ω(d + log n) left open in the active learning literature. In fact, our algorithm solves
     the more general problem of learning a Boolean function f over n elements which is monotone
     under at least one of D provided orderings of these elements. Our technical insight is to exploit the
     structure in these orderings to essentially perform a binary search in parallel rather than considering
     each ordering sequentially, and we believe our approach may be of broader interest.
          Furthermore, we use our exact learning algorithm to obtain nearly optimal algorithms for PAC-
     learning. We show that O(min(D + log(1/ε), 1/ε) · log D) queries suffice to learn f within error ε,
     even in a setting when f can be adversarially corrupted on a cε-fraction of points, for a sufficiently
     small constant c. This bound is optimal up to a log D factor, including in the realizable setting.


1. Introduction
Halfspaces, or linear threshold functions (LTFs), are one of the most fundamental and well-studied
objects in computer science and geometry, with numerous applications in machine learning, opti-
mization, and beyond. The halfspace with normal vector u ∈ S d−1 and threshold t ∈ R bisects Rd
into two regions, classifying x using the rule 1(⟨u, x⟩ > t). In this work, we consider the following
halfspace learning question. Given a dataset X ⊂ Rd partitioned into two classes by an unknown
halfspace f : Rd → {0, 1}, we are allowed to adaptively query the label f (x) for any x ∈ X and

     With point synthesis, there is an information-theoretic lower bound of Ω(d log n) queries and
there has been extensive work on obtaining upper bounds auf der Heide (1984); Meiser (1993); Car-

query algorithm due to Hopkins et al. (2020). However, the ability to synthesize and query arbi-
trary data points is a strong assumption which may be infeasible in many settings, and our primary
motivation in this work is to investigate when and how this can be avoided. The bad news is that,
in general, without point synthesis no non-trivial algorithm is possible due to the following sim-
ple Ω(n) lower bound observed by Dasgupta (2004) which holds even in two dimensions: for a
set X of n distinct points on the unit circle, it is straightforward to design a family of halfspaces
{fx : x ∈ X} such that fx uniquely assigns fx (x) = 1 among all points in X, and thus one must
query every point in order to learn every label2 .
Learning halfspaces optimally in bounded directions. The above lower bound comes from the
fact that there are an unbounded number of directions the halfspace can be in, and each direction
can be used to separate a single point in X from the rest. Various ways of circumventing this lower
bound have been considered in the literature (see Section 1.2); however, to do so without weakening
the assumption of a worst-case point set or adding point synthesis, it is necessary to bound the
number of directions parameterizing the halfspace. It is not too hard to see that if D ≤ n directions
are allowed, then the above argument gives an Ω(D) lower bound and Ω(log n) queries are needed
(to determine the threshold) even in one dimension, leading to an Ω(D +log n) lower bound. On the
other hand it is not too challenging to design an algorithm using O(D log n) queries by projecting X
along each allowed direction, and performing a binary search independently using the ordering on
X induced by each projection. This algorithm simply exploits the fact that the labels are monotone
along the correct direction. In fact, even for the simple special case of axis-aligned halfspaces
(depth-one decision trees) in Rd , there is a gap of O(d log n) vs. Ω(d + log n) that exists in the
active learning literature Hanneke and Yang (2015). We investigate the core algorithmic question
underlying this gap: can we exploit structure beyond monotonicity of the labels to go beyond a
naive, independent application of binary search? We give an affirmative answer, designing a new
algorithm that achieves the optimal O(D + log n) query complexity, thus closing this gap.

Main application: decision stumps, or axis-aligned halfspaces. A natural class of halfspaces
with bounded directions is the class of axis-aligned halfspaces. Such functions are equivalent to
decision stumps (depth-one decision trees), which classify data by thresholding with respect to a
single feature. They are the basic building blocks of decision trees, commonly used in practice as
base learners in ensemble learning techniques such as bagging and boosting Holte (1993); Oliver
and Hand (1994); Banihashem et al. (2023). For learning decision stumps over arbitrary point sets in
Rd , there is a gap of O(d log n) vs. Ω(d + log n) left open in the active learning literature Hanneke
and Yang (2015). As a direct corollary of our main result, we obtain a deterministic algorithm using
O(d + log n) queries, closing the book on this fundamental concept class.
     Beyond depth one, there is a large body of research on decision tree learning over the Boolean
hypercube, {0, 1}d (e.g. Blanc et al. (2022, 2020); Bshouty and Haddad-Zaknoon (2019); Ehren-
feucht and Haussler (1989)); however, we note that there is an Ω(n) query lower bound for learning
Boolean decision trees of depth at least two4 when the domain X ⊂ Rd is arbitrary. On the other
hand, an alternative generalization is the problem of learning multi-class decision trees, where each
leaf must correspond to a distinct label, over arbitrary X ⊂ Rd . We do not know of any prior works
studying this question and we believe this may be an interesting direction for future work.
     Beyond the axis-aligned setting, a more general class of halfspaces where our results have im-
plications are sparse discrete halfspaces: given a sparsity parameter s ∈ {1, . . . , d}, suppose we
restrict the normal vector to lie in {−1, 0, 1}d (or a larger hypergrid) with at most s non-zero coor-

a learner with query complexity dO(s) + O(log n) for exactly learning such a halfspace over an
arbitrary point set X ⊂ Rd . This notion of sparse halfspaces has been considered in numerous
works (e.g. Matulef et al. (2009), Abasi et al. (2016), Mazumdar and Sangwan (2025) for a small
sampling), but not for the problem we consider, to the best of our knowledge.

1.1. Results
We now state our main results. Given X ⊂ Rd and a set V = {u1 , . . . , uD } ⊂ S d−1 of D

1.2. Related Work
We study active learning in the pool-based setting: we are given access to a set X ⊂ Rd of n
unlabeled points and may adaptively query the labels of these points Settles (2009). For arbitrary
non-homogeneous halfspaces in the exact, no-synthesis setting, there is a strong worst-case lower
bound on the number of queries needed to label every point in X: even if the points lie on a circle
in R2 , the worst-case label complexity is Ω(n) queries Dasgupta (2004).
     There are various ways to circumvent this barrier. One way is to introduce additional assump-
tions about the label function and the data: assume that the halfspace goes through the origin and
that the data is drawn from a nice distribution. For example, standard choices are the uniform dis-
tribution over the unit sphere or a log-concave distribution Dasgupta et al. (2009); Balcan and Long
(2013). Margin-based approaches exploit additional structure near the decision boundary, such as
margin separability, small boundary mass, or noise conditions relating label uncertainty to distance
from the boundary Balcan et al. (2007); Gonen et al. (2013). In a related online selective sampling
setting, margin information can also be used to decide when to query labels and to obtain mistake
bounds in terms of hinge or soft-margin losses Cesa-Bianchi et al. (2006). Finally, another common
way to avoid the lower bound is to strengthen the query model, for example by allowing point syn-
thesis or membership queries, where the learner may query labels of points outside the given pool
Hopkins et al. (2020); Diakonikolas et al. (2024). The downside to membership queries is that, in
practice, synthetic data may not have a sensible label Baum and Lang (1992); Dasgupta (2004).
     This work parametrizes the hardness of learning halfspaces in a new, purely combinatorial way:
we restrict the class of halfspaces to structured subclasses with bounded directionality. We assume
that the normal vectors of the halfspaces are contained in a set of D known directions. Importantly,
this assumption does not restrict the data in any way, admitting arbitrary, worst-case point sets. We
also do not assume access to the stronger membership query oracle.
     The family of decision stumps is a canonical example of halfspaces with bounded directionality.
For exact learning of decision stumps, prior general bounds imply an O(d log n) upper bound and
a Ω(d + log n) lower bound Hanneke and Yang (2015); our O(d + log n) bound closes this gap.
In spirit, our algorithm resembles classic active learning algorithms like CAL and A2 , which only
query points that lead to certain progress Cohn et al. (1994); Balcan et al. (2006). However, our
algorithm is more aggressive in the sense that not all progress is equal Dasgupta (2011). Our
algorithm identifies and exploits more informative points to achieve optimal query complexity.

Appendix A. Approximate Learning
In this section we consider ε-learning a halfspace over an arbitrary set X ⊂ Rd of n points whose
normal vector comes from a known set V = {u1 , . . . , uD } ⊂ S d−1 of D unit vectors. We prove
items (3) and (2) of Theorem 1 in Section A.1 and Section A.2, respectively.
    Our algorithms in this section crucially invoke our algorithm for exactly learning shuffled mono-
tone functions obtained in Section 2.1. This algorithm is combined with a randomized binary search
procedure which gives a tolerant learner in the 1-dimensional setting, along with a basic technique
from property testing of monotone functions, and a careful probabilistic analysis.
    Throughout the section, let M denote the class of monotone Boolean functions over [n], and
for f : [n] → {0, 1}, let d(f, M) = ming∈M ∥f − g∥1 denote the minimum Hamming distance of
f to any monotone function. Note that here ∥f − h∥1 = |{j ∈ [n] : f (j) ̸= h(j)}| · n−1 . We use
the notation hS to denote the restriction of h to a subset S of its domain.

A.1. Tolerant Learning
The following lemma gives an optimal c-tolerant algorithm for learning monotone functions in 1-
dimension, for sufficiently small constant c. We use this algorithm as a subroutine for our ε-learners
